proves: above the radius threshold a dashed border runs one fitted pattern round the closed path -- the arcs carry gaps, the loop's length is the CENTRE path, and the slack is scattered as narrow gaps rather than left at an end
checkable: 240x48 on white, one box filling it with `border: 4px dashed #000000` and `border-radius: 8px`. Radius 8 at width 4 is ABOVE the threshold - the branch is `radius > width`, because the inner radius is `radius - width` and at or below it the inner corner is square. Read the TOP band at row y=2; the straight portion runs from x=8 to x=231, and a pixel is ink below 128 in the red channel.
chrome: the straight portion's ink spans x=8..229, which is 222 of the 224 available: NOT flush at both ends, where the square box beside this one is flush at both. The runs from the box's left edge: `off:7@0 on:9@7 off:4@16 on:8@20 off:4@28 on:8@32 off:4@40 on:8@44 off:4@52 on:8@56 off:4@64 on:8@68 off:3@76 ...` - dash 8 and gap 4 as on the square box, but beginning inside the arc rather than at the tangent.
chrome_at_the_arcs: walked along the centreline of the band rather than across it, because a band row crosses a curve obliquely and can only ever show one short mark. Top-left quarter, 9.4 long: `first-ink@0 on:4.4 off:4.1 on:1.0`. Top-right: `first-ink@3.1 off:3.1 on:6.3`. The arcs are DASHED, on the same rhythm as the sides. Sixteen samples per pixel: at four the two radii read identically. From `dashed-arc-8-top-left` and `-top-right` in `crates/meo-canvas/tests/assets/chrome/border-rhythm.tsv`.
status: OUR RENDER, pinned as a disagreement with Chrome at the WRAP alone. NOT a target image. Everything else in it is measured against Chrome and agrees, including the loop's length and the whole straight run. **This image has been accepted three times and re-measured each time**, because the renderer moved underneath it twice while it was being certified: the perimeter fit landed after the first acceptance and the anchored contour after the second, and the fixture failed loudly on both. An accepted image is a measurement, and a measurement taken while the renderer was moving is not one - so re-measure before re-accepting, never diff and assume. That the pin cost one re-measure each time instead of certifying a picture of a renderer that no longer exists is the whole reason it is written this way. `borders-per-edge` is the counter-example: it certified two corners while they were wrong, twice, because a render was accepted as though it were a reference.
disagreement: ONE difference, at the WRAP alone, and it is a threshold reading rather than a geometry difference - see `why_the_wrap_is_not_pinned_as_a_defect`. From x=8 to x=231 this image and Chrome's are identical, boundary for boundary: `on:8@8 off:4@16 on:8@20 off:4@28 ...` in both. The five-pixel phase difference this field used to carry is GONE - the contour is traced from the top-left tangent, so the pattern starts there because the path does rather than by an offset. What is left at y=2: Chrome reads `off:7@0 on:9@7` where we read `off:2@0 on:3@2 off:3@5 on:8@8`. Both are reading the same arc mark and the same anchored dash through a single row.
the_loop_is_the_centre_path: MEASURED on both sides, and it is the one thing a closed dashed loop can be got wrong by a whole mark. A rounded rect's loop is `2(w + h) - r(8 - 2*pi)`. For this box the CENTRE path (236x44, radius 6 - the radius is inset with the rectangle) is 549.70 and the OUTER path (240x48, radius 8) is 562.27; over a period of 12 those predict 45.81 and 46.86 marks, which round to 46 and 47. **A full perimeter walk of this image counts 46.** Chrome answers the same way on the box its own table was measured in: `dashed-perimeter-w4-r8` on 137x120 predicts 40.64 centre against 41.69 outer, and Chrome's row counts 41. Both boxes, both renderers, the centre path. Note that Chrome fits the OUTER straight length per side on a SQUARE box - see `borders-dashed-square` - so the two are different mechanisms and not a contradiction.
counting_marks_on_a_closed_loop: The walk reports 47 runs of ink here and Chrome's reports 42, and both numbers are one too many. A closed walk starts partway through a mark and ends in the same one, so the first and last runs are a single mark split by the start point: ours are `on:3.0` and `on:5.9`, Chrome's `on:8.0` and `on:1.0`, and each pair sums to about one 8-long dash. Joining them gives 46 and 41 -- and the check that they are right is that a closed loop has AS MANY GAPS AS MARKS, which only holds after the join.
the_pair_is_the_point: either picture alone is a dashed box. What the two say together is that the behaviour CHANGES with the radius: the square box is fitted per side, against the OUTER straight length, and is flush at both ends of every edge; this one is a single fitted run around the closed CENTRE path with no flushness at any tangent. Do not read this image's straight portion as flush - it spans all 224 pixels, but because a mark straddles the tangent rather than because the side was fitted, and the mark count is what tells the two apart.
why_the_wrap_is_not_pinned_as_a_defect: Because it is not a fit difference at all: both renderers draw the SAME mark on the arc and disagree only about which of its pixels clear a threshold at the one row a band scan reads. Measured, not argued. Chrome's arc region at radius 8, x=0..17, with `#` under 128, `+` between and `.` above: `y=1 .......#########`, `y=2 .++....#########`, `y=3 .##+...#########`, `y=4 +###+..+`. Ours over the same region: `y=1 ...#+...########`, `y=2 ..###...########`, `y=3 .#####..########`, `y=4 +#####`. BOTH carry a coherent mark on the arc, widening as the curve turns through four rows; it is not a blip on one row in either. **The clinching row is Chrome's own at radius 6**, where the fit is exact and both renderers agree: its first straight mark reads NINE pixels wide at y=0 and EIGHT at y=2 - Chrome disagreeing with itself by one pixel between two rows of one mark, which is the whole size of the radius-8 disagreement. A mark's leading edge near a tangent is a curved boundary, and which pixels of it cross 128 depends on the row and on the radius. Two hypotheses died getting here and both were mine or Agent One's: that the loop was fitted to a length a unit short (dead - the fit is EXACT at radius 5 and 6, and a systematic underestimate cannot be absent at two radii and present at one), and that Chrome is a unit off an exact closure everywhere so it is shared Skia behaviour (dead - Chrome closes exactly at radius 5 and 6, `on:8@5` and `on:8@6`).
what_cannot_be_measured_here: The length Skia actually dashes along. The hypothesis for our early arrival is that a path's measured length runs a shade under its geometry because conics are flattened to quads, which would make the loop a little less than the exact 549.70. It is not checkable from this image and it is not checkable from the renderer: `meo-skia-canvas` 0.11.0 exposes `measure_text` and `measure_text_extents` and no path length at all. The difference between the two candidates is 3.950 against 3.928 per gap across 46 gaps, an order of magnitude under what a run quantised to whole pixels can resolve - so no number this harness reports for it would be a measurement.
three_hypotheses_died_here: Recorded because a reader who meets only the surviving explanation will re-derive one of these. One from each of us, none surviving contact with a row. (1) SHARED SKIA CONSTANT - that both engines sit a unit off an exact closure, so it is one rasteriser's behaviour seen twice. Killed by `border-rhythm.tsv`: Chrome closes EXACTLY at radius 5 and 6, `on:8@5` and `on:8@6`, on the same branch. (2) CONIC FLATTENING - that a path's measured length runs under its geometry because conics flatten to quads, making our loop a shade short. Killed by our own render at those radii: the fit is exact at 5 and 6, and a systematic underestimate cannot be absent at two radii and present at one. (3) DIFFERING PATTERNS INSIDE THE CORNER - that Chrome closes its loop with a dash where we close with a gap. Killed by reading Chrome's arc region across rows rather than at y=2 alone: Chrome carries the same coherent arc mark we do, through four rows. What survived is the dullest of the four and the only one with evidence internal to a single renderer.
